The northwest corner is the tile's address in lon/lat; the centre is its representative point. They differ by half a tile — at z15 in New York, ~460 m — and choosing the wrong one is a quiet, mappable error.
Tile x maps to longitude by pure proportion (x ÷ 2^z × 360 − 180); latitude needs the inverse Mercator (atan of sinh) — the asymmetry that makes this page a calculator rather than a ruler.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
Latitude/longitude from tile numbers via the inverse slippy-map formulas — longitude linearly, latitude through atan(sinh(·)), for the tile's corner or centre.
Which map standard does it use?
The slippy-map standard (Web Mercator, 256-px tiles) shared by OSM, Google and MapLibre.
Can I use this in production GIS?
The formulas are the production standard itself — yes for web-mapping work.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — tile systems are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — tiles and pixels quantise; decimals beyond the cell are decoration.
Which corner?
Northwest by convention (the tile's origin). Centre available as the representative point; full bounds on the sibling page.
TMS y-flip?
Invert the flip first — y_xyz = 2^z − 1 − y_tms — then convert.
Fractional tiles?
Tile addresses are integers by definition; fractional zooms in libraries pick the integer level beneath for addressing.
Does it recover my original point?
Only to tile precision — the point's exact position inside the tile is gone after tiling, which is the system's design, not a defect.
Polar rows?
The top row inverts to the 85.0511° cap — the grid's edge, faithfully returned.
